output.normalized_title: redis-cluster: PostgreSQL active connection pool reached 100% (250/250) (redis-cluster)

output.classification_reasoning: The incident reports that the PostgreSQL active connection pool reached its maximum capacity (250/250) while being accessed via the redis-cluster service. This indicates a saturation of database connections, a classic database resource exhaustion scenario, rather than a network, authentication, or application code bug. The involvement of redis-cluster as a dependent service adds a layer of indirect impact (telemetry spike), but the root cause remains the database connection pool limit. Resolving such issues typically requires analyzing connection pooling configuration, query performance, and possibly scaling the database tier, which involves multiple components and coordination across services. Hence, the failure is classified as a database_problem with a moderate level of operational complexity.

prerequisites: Root access or AWS SSO role ProdOperations
output.security_notes: Do not terminate primary node without promoting read-replica first. Verify write freeze before reboot.

recurring_patterns.symptom_pattern: redis-cluster: PostgreSQL active connection pool reached 100% (250/250)

diagnostic_stage_assessment.notes: No exact historical incident or error signature match. Only similarity is the database_problem category and the same service (redis-clUSTER). Further investigation required to confirm root cause.

output.governing_sla_rule: Tier-1 service impacting >= 500 users, or cross-tier impact >= 2,000 users.
output.justification: The incident affects 3,500 users, far exceeding the 2,000‑user cross‑tier threshold defined in the SLA rule. Although the service tier is Tier‑2, the rule applies across tiers when the user count surpasses 2,000. The outage duration of 79 minutes is significant but does not alone trigger a higher severity; the primary driver is the large user impact. Therefore, the deterministic rule recommends SEV‑2, and this aligns with the SLA policy for high‑impact incidents affecting thousands of users.

remediation_steps.title: Validate Access and Kubernetes Context
remediation_steps.description: Ensure the operator has the required ProdOperations role and that kubectl is pointed at the production cluster in us‑east‑1.
verification: AWS identity matches ProdOperations role
kubectl context output contains 'prod-us-east-1'

remediation_steps.title: Assess Redis Connection Pool Utilization
remediation_steps.description: Query the Redis metrics to confirm the connection pool saturation and identify which pods are at 100% usage.
commands: kubectl -n redis get pods -l app=redis-cluster -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}:{.status.phase}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl -n redis exec $(kubectl -n redis get pod -l app=redis-cluster -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli INFO clients
verification: Metrics show 250/250 connections on at least one pod
No other error signatures appear in pod logs

remediation_steps.title: Graceful Rolling Restart of Redis Pods
remediation_steps.description: Perform a rolling restart to free stale connections while preserving data integrity. The runbook requires promoting a read‑replica before any primary node disruption.
commands: # Promote a read‑replica to primary if not already done
kubectl -n redis exec $(kubectl -n redis get pod -l role=replica -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- redis-cli REPLICAOF NO ONE
verification: All pods transition through Terminating → Running and report READY=1/1
Post‑restart `INFO clients` shows connection count < 70% of max
Service health endpoint returns 200 OK

remediation_steps.title: Increase Connection Pool Limit (Optional)
remediation_steps.description: If usage trends remain high, adjust the PostgreSQL connection pool size in the Redis‑Postgres bridge configuration and redeploy.
verification: ConfigMap reflects new `max_connections` value
Bridge pods restart successfully
Connection pool metric stabilizes below 80% of new limit

remediation_steps.title: Post‑Remediation Health Audit
remediation_steps.description: Run synthetic health checks and verify that error rates have returned to baseline.
commands: kubectl -n redis logs -l app=redis-cluster --since=5m | grep -i error || true
verification: Health endpoint returns `{ "status": "OK" }`
Log grep returns no recent error entries

rollback_plan.overall_strategy: Revert the Redis StatefulSet to the previous revision and restore the original connection‑pool configuration. Verify service stability before removing the rollback.

steps.description: Undo the rolling restart to the prior replica set revision.
verification: Pods return to the previous revision number
`kubectl -n redis get sts redis-cluster -o jsonpath='{.status.currentRevision}'` matches pre‑restart revision

steps.description: Restore original connection‑pool ConfigMap if it was modified.
commands: kubectl -n redis get configmap redis-pg-bridge-config -o yaml > /tmp/backup-config.yaml
kubectl -n redis edit configmap redis-pg-bridge-config # revert `max_connections` to 250
verification: ConfigMap shows `max_connections: 250`
Bridge pods restart and report READY=1/1

commands: kubectl -n redis logs -l app=redis-cluster --since=5m | grep -i error || true
verification: Health endpoint returns OK
No new error logs appear

prerequisite_checks: Operator credentials verified for ProdOperations role
AWS SSO session active and MFA completed
Rollback procedure documented and approved by change manager
safety_verification.notes: All actions are reversible, require no data loss, and respect the runbook security note to promote a read‑replica before any primary node impact.
